title: Photomultiplier dynodes: electron-multiplying gain register on every bitline
idea: Forced connection to a photomultiplier/EMCCD dynode chain: between cell and sense amp insert a short serial register of 8-10 high-field transfer gates in the SA strip, each adding ~1.2x impact-ionization gain, so a 1 fF cell's ~3,000 signal electrons arrive at the latch as ~15,000-20,000. The register is clocked only during the sense phase.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): 5-6x pre-latch gain lets Cs fall from ~5 fF to ~1 fF, cutting pillar AR from ~70:1 toward ~20:1 or making small-cap 3D tiers viable; risks are excess gain noise and the high clock voltage.

title: AM radio dial: frequency-multiplexed resonator readout of 64 bitlines
idea: Like superconducting-qubit dispersive readout or an AM dial, give each of 64 bitlines a tiny BEOL LC resonator at its own frequency, all coupled to one feedline; the post-charge-sharing bitline voltage tunes a varactor and shifts its resonance by a few MHz. One broadband comb probe plus a digital channelizer reads all 64 at once, and a minimal pass-gate driver writes the decoded value back.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): replaces 64 full latch sense amps with one wideband receiver plus 64 write-back switches, potentially 3-5x less SA-strip area if resonators fit in upper metal over the array.

title: Cochlear hair cell: Hopf-bifurcation oscillator as sense amplifier
idea: Outer hair cells reach huge gain for faint sounds by sitting just below an oscillation onset (a Hopf bifurcation). Bias a 3-4 transistor local oscillator per bitline pair right at onset; the small charge-sharing signal pushes it into oscillation at phase 0 or phase pi, and a phase detector latches the bit before a restore driver writes back.
why: Capacitor charge wall: near-bifurcation compressive gain could resolve ~10-15 mV instead of ~60-100 mV, so Cs could drop ~3-5x or bitlines double in length, removing half the SA strips (~10% of die).

title: Electrometer umbrella: bootstrapped guard lines erase bitline capacitance
idea: Electrometers hide cable capacitance under a guard 'umbrella' driven by a unity-gain copy of the signal. Route a guard trace in the metal level directly above each bitline (stacked, so no pitch cost) and drive it during charge sharing from a per-pair source follower that tracks the bitline, so the bitline-to-overlayer and contact coupling sees almost no voltage change.
why: Transfer ratio Cs/(Cs+C_BL): removing ~30-40% of effective bitline capacitance raises read signal ~1.5x, worth ~1.5 fF of Cs (lower capacitor AR) or ~50% longer bitlines with fewer SA strips.

title: Seashell roar: chopped, dithered comparator voting senses sub-offset signals
idea: A seashell turns random noise into a perceptible 'ocean': use stochastic resonance. After charge sharing, sample the bitline onto a small isolated cap, then fire a minimum-size comparator 8 times against a reference dithered by an on-die junction-noise source, swapping inputs on alternate firings (chopping) to cancel offset, and majority-vote in a 3-bit counter before restore.
why: Sense-amp area: minimum-size comparators with ~30 mV offset can resolve ~10 mV signals statistically, so SA transistors shrink ~4x in area (SA strips are a large share of the ~49% periphery), at a cost of ~2-3 ns latency.

title: Strowger stepper: token-passing wordline drivers replace local row decoders
idea: A Strowger telephone switch steps one contact per pulse instead of decoding a full number. For streaming and AI traffic that walks rows in order, make each wordline driver a bootstrapped 4-transistor dynamic shift stage (as in LCD gate-on-array drivers) passing a single token, and keep a coarse random-access decoder only every 32 rows to jump the token.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): removes the row-address bus and per-row NAND decode from the local driver strip, perhaps 20-30% of decoder area; random jumps cost up to 31 extra clock steps, acceptable for sequential tiers.

title: Ice-cream sandwich: U.S. mature-node periphery wafers bonded to arrays
idea: Split every die into an array-only wafer (cells, bitlines, capacitors) and a periphery wafer (SAs, decoders, pumps, I/O) built on existing U.S. 28-40 nm logic lines, joined by wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding with one bond per bitline staggered along its length (a ~50 um bitline has ~1.5 um2 of footprint, room for a 1 um-pitch pad).
why: Capital and U.S. manufacturability: the ~49% periphery needs no EUV and moves to depreciated U.S. fabs, freeing ~40% of scarce DRAM-fab wafer area per bit and letting new array-only fabs skip most logic steps (~30% less capex).

title: Lego studs: open standard for array-to-periphery bonded interfaces
idea: Lego bricks from any box snap together because the stud is standardized. Publish an open, royalty-free 'memory stud' spec covering bond pitch, per-bitline-group pad maps, voltage domains, test hooks and known-good-die protocol, so array-only wafers from any fab can bond to periphery wafers from any foundry; tie CHIPS-style funding to compliance.
why: Capital and supply diversity: breaks the 3-vendor vertical integration, letting U.S. logic foundries and new array specialists each enter with roughly half the capex of a full DRAM fab.

title: Tuning fork: analog trim cell retunes every sense amp offset
idea: Like filing a tuning fork to pitch, each SA gets one DRAM-style trim capacitor on its tail node; at power-up and then every refresh window the bitlines are shorted and a calibration loop pumps charge onto that cap until the latch flips at zero input, so the offset correction is stored as analog charge and refreshed like data.
why: Periphery area: SA devices are upsized only to beat Pelgrom mismatch; nulling ~80% of offset lets them shrink ~4x in area (SA strip ~25-35% smaller) or halves the bitline signal needed, easing the capacitor wall.

title: Honeycomb: brick-bond mat tiling shares each sense strip three ways
idea: Bees get the most area per wall with hexagons. Lay mats in a Manhattan-friendly brick-bond pattern that approximates hexagons so each SA strip segment borders three mats, and give each SA 3:1 isolation switches; only one of the three mats is active per strip at a time, versus 2:1 sharing today.
why: Periphery area: SA strips are ~20-25% of die; three-way sharing removes ~1/3 of SAs per bit, ~7% die area saved, at the cost of activation constraints between neighbouring mats.

title: Smoke detector: leaky analog charge counters catch row hammer
idea: Smoke builds up in an ionization chamber until the alarm trips. Give each group of 4 rows one tiny capacitor in the wordline-driver strip that gets a fixed charge packet per activation and leaks with a ~64 ms time constant; a comparator trips at ~500 activations' worth of charge and queues a targeted neighbour refresh.
why: Row hammer (fact 9, ~1k activation threshold): replaces SRAM counter tables and TRR logic with ~3 transistors plus 1 cap per 4 rows, monitors every row so it cannot be evaded by many-sided patterns, and costs <1% die.

title: Canary in coal mine: leaky sentinel cells set refresh pace
idea: Place 8 canary cells per mat whose access transistors are drawn ~15% shorter so they leak ~3x faster than the worst real cell; during idle the SA checks them every few ms and the mat is refreshed only after a canary flips, so the refresh period tracks real temperature and process instead of a fixed 32-64 ms worst case.
why: Refresh tax (fact 3: 16-33% of idle power, 10-20% of bandwidth): typical dies and temperatures retain far longer than spec, so mat-level adaptive refresh can stretch intervals 2-4x safely.

title: Rubik's cube: re-keyed permutation shuffles physical row neighbors
idea: Twist the cube so neighbours change: put a 3-round keyed Feistel shuffle on the 6 low row-address bits in front of each mat's decoder and re-key it incrementally, swapping one row pair per refresh command, so logically adjacent rows map to unpredictable physical neighbours that keep moving.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): attackers cannot aim aggressors at a victim, removing most per-row counter area; cost is a few hundred gates per bank plus one row swap per refresh slot (~1% bandwidth).

title: Abacus beads: successive-approximation sensing reads two bits per cell
idea: Read like sliding abacus beads one rank at a time: after charge sharing a 2-step SAR sense amp compares against a mid reference for the MSB, then switches in a binary-weighted half-step reference capacitor to resolve the LSB, and a 4-level write driver restores one of four voltages.
why: Density and cost per bit ~2x with the same capacitor, but it needs ~3-4x signal, so it must pair with a gain or low-C_BL idea; adds ~20% SA area.

title: Chess clock: time-domain race arbiter replaces voltage latch sense amp
idea: Turn voltage into time like a chess clock: the bitline and reference each set the current of a starved inverter discharging a node, and a mutual-exclusion arbiter (first press locks out the other) latches whichever crosses first before a restore driver writes back.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10) and SA area: delay gain turns ~20 mV into ~100 ps and keeps working at 0.5-0.6 V where cross-coupled latches fail; the arbiter is ~4 transistors plus 2 delay cells.

title: Magnifying glass: one-transistor local preamp every sixteen cells
idea: A magnifying glass enlarges the signal before the eye sees it: split each bitline into 16-cell local segments of ~1 fF; the cell shares charge with this tiny segment (about +/-300 mV), which drives the gate of one segment transistor that discharges the long global bitline, while a separate write-back transistor restores.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): transfer ratio rises from ~0.1 to ~0.8, so Cs can drop to ~1 fF (AR ~15:1) and 3D tiers can use tiny capacitors; costs 2 transistors per 16 cells (~10% array overhead).

title: Jacquard loom: coincident half-select tier addressing, no 3D staircase
idea: A Jacquard loom lifts any thread pattern by crossing hooks and cords. In 3D DRAM, replace the per-tier staircase contacts with a tier-select plate per level and a gate line per vertical pillar, each driven to about half the turn-on voltage, so only the tier-by-pillar intersection conducts, as in coincident-current core memory.
why: 3D DRAM blockers (fact 2): staircase area and per-tier drivers grow linearly with tiers; coincident selection needs N+M drivers for NxM cells and drops the staircase etch loop (~5-10 litho/etch steps at 32+ tiers).

title: Bunk bed: oxide thin-film decoders stacked above the cell array
idea: Put the decoders upstairs like a bunk bed: build row predecoders, wordline-driver pull-ups and column-select logic from BEOL W-doped In2O3 or IGZO thin-film transistors (as in LCD gate-on-array drivers) directly over the array at <=400 C, connected down by vias, leaving only sense amps in silicon.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): decoders and drivers are ~15-20% of die; stacking them gives ~15% more bits per wafer with no EUV, and oxide TFTs tolerate the 3 V wordline swing.

title: Post-it notes: module controller remaps bad rows, fuses removed
idea: Instead of burning fixes into each die, stick notes on the module: dies ship without e-fuse banks or redundancy-steering comparators, and the CXL/buffer controller keeps a remap table of bad rows and columns found at test (stored in SPD flash) that redirects to spare rows pooled across every die on the module.
why: Periphery area and yield: fuse banks and spare-steering logic are ~3-6% of die; pooling spares at module level also lifts usable-die yield by a few percent.

title: Potluck cookbook: open-source, silicon-proven DRAM periphery IP commons
idea: A potluck works because everyone shares recipes. Fund an open-source library of DRAM periphery blocks (sense amps with offset calibration, row-hammer trackers, pumps, LPDDR/DDR5 PHYs) with silicon-proven layouts on U.S. 28/22 nm processes, so startups and foundries can build memory dies without decades of trade-secret circuit know-how.
why: Capital and U.S. manufacturability: periphery know-how is a hidden entry barrier; shared IP could cut a new entrant's design cost from ~$500M to ~$50-100M and save ~2 years.

title: Egg grading: on-die margin sweep sells refresh-grade memory tiers
idea: Grade dies like eggs (AA, A, B): every die runs an on-die sweep of SA reference offset steps and retention waits, then is sold as a 'cool-datacenter' grade (256 ms refresh at <=60 C), a standard grade or a 'hot' grade; operators who run cold buy parts needing 4x less refresh.
why: Usable supply and refresh tax (fact 3): turns retention spread into priced tiers, recovering 10-20% bandwidth on graded parts and monetizing margin now wasted on worst-case design.

title: Noise-cancelling headphones: cross-neutralization capacitors cancel bitline coupling
idea: Like active noise cancellation, inject anti-noise: each SA gets small neutralization capacitors from both neighbours' complementary latch nodes, so as an adjacent bitline develops its signal, an equal anti-phase charge is injected, nulling bitline-to-bitline coupling at 24 nm pitch.
why: Signal margin (fact 1): coupling from opposite-data neighbours steals ~20-30% of read signal; recovering it is worth ~1 fF of Cs or ~25% longer bitlines with fewer SA strips.

title: Suspension bridge: mid-span regenerator towers double bitline length
idea: A suspension bridge spans far with a few towers. Insert a stripped-down 4-transistor single-ended regenerator (no column switch, equalizer or I/O, compared against a shared mid-rail reference) at the midpoint of each bitline, so bitlines can be 2x longer while the full SA sits only at the end.
why: Periphery area: halving the number of full SA strips (~20% of die) while towers cost ~1/3 of an SA saves ~6-8% die area.

title: Regenerative brakes: LC-resonant wordline drive returns wordline charge
idea: Like a hybrid car's brakes refilling the battery, connect the selected wordline through its driver to a bank-level spiral inductor so it swings to ~3 V resonantly from a tank capacitor, and on close let the charge ring back into the tank instead of dumping it to ground; the ~30%-efficient charge pump then only tops up losses.
why: Wordline and pump losses are ~15-25% of activation energy; ~85% recovery plus no pump overhead cuts that component ~10x; inductor ~0.05 mm2 per bank.

title: Canal locks with side basins: stepwise adiabatic bitline charging
idea: Water-saving canal locks fill and drain in steps from side basins and reuse most of the water. Raise the sense-amp rails (and so 8k bitlines) in 6-8 steps from on-die tank capacitors at intermediate voltages, and on precharge return each step's charge to its basin, so the supply only tops up resistive losses.
why: Bitline CV2 is the largest activation term (facts 8, 10); N-step charging cuts dissipation ~N, so 8 steps plus basin return of the discharging bitline gives ~6-10x; tank caps reuse DRAM's own capacitor process; ~2 ns extra latency.

title: Totem pole: four voltage-stacked subarrays reuse one charge packet
idea: Stack four subarrays' sense-amp domains in series like a totem pole (0.75-1.0 V, 0.5-0.75 V, 0.25-0.5 V, 0-0.25 V); charge drained from the top domain's bitlines becomes the supply current of the next, so one packet does four activations' work, with small push-pull regulators balancing the domains during wide simultaneous fetches.
why: Supply energy per activation drops ~4x from charge reuse and swing is 0.25 V instead of 1 V, ~10x combined, but only if offset-trimmed SAs can sense the smaller stored signal.

title: Tweezers: 64-cell micro-row activation ends page overfetch
idea: Pick one item with tweezers instead of scooping the tray: split each wordline into 64-cell micro-rows with a 2-transistor local AND driver (global wordline x column-group select), so an access opens and senses only the 64-512 cells requested, not an 8 kb page.
why: Destructive read with 128x overfetch (fact 8, ~5.9 pJ per useful bit): sensing energy per useful bit falls ~16-100x, so total access energy drops >10x; costs ~5-8% array area for local drivers.

title: Radiant floor tiles: sense amps under array enable short, low-voltage bitlines
idea: Lay sense amps under the mats like heating tiles under a floor, on a logic layer joined by 0.3-0.5 um-pitch hybrid bonds (one per bitline), so bitlines shrink from ~512 to ~128 cells; the ~4x lower C_BL triples read signal, and that margin is spent cutting VARY from 1.0 V to ~0.5 V.
why: Bitline energy scales with C_BL x VARY2: 4x lower C times 4x lower V2 gives ~10-16x less array energy per activation, and SA area stops costing die area (fact 7).

title: Library whisper: virtual-ground charge-transfer sensing keeps bitlines frozen
idea: In a library nobody raises their voice: hold every bitline at a fixed potential with a cascode charge-transfer amplifier so it never swings; the cell's charge flows through into a ~0.5 fF integrating node at the SA, giving a large local voltage, and restore pushes the same charge back through the cascode.
why: The ~100 fF bitline never charges or discharges, so bitline CV2, the dominant activation term, disappears; only cell charge moves, ~10-20x less array energy; risk is cascode speed and offset at 24 nm pitch.

title: Matchstick: consume-once reads with decoupled sense amps skip restore
idea: A match is used once: add an isolation gate so the SA latches from a +/-100 mV bitline signal without driving the bitline rail to rail, and add a READ-CONSUME command; for data the host marks read-once (streamed KV cache, network buffers, transpose scratch) the row is left destroyed and marked free, so neither full swing nor restore happens.
why: Full-swing restore is >70% of activation energy; consume reads cut array energy ~10x and halve tRAS; needs a JEDEC/CXL command and OS tracking of dead rows.

title: Coffee straw: partial-charge sip reads defer restore for many reads
idea: Sip through a straw instead of draining the cup: drive the wordline only into weak inversion for ~5 ns so ~10% of the cell's charge (~0.25 fC) flows into a clamped bitline and onto a 0.5 fF integrating sense node (~0.5 V signal); the cell stays readable and is restored only every ~5 sips or at refresh.
why: Removes per-read restore, full bitline swing and the 3 V wordline pulse: ~10x less energy per read for read-mostly data such as AI weights; risks are weak-inversion variability and tracking a sip count per row.

title: Crystal radio: tunnel-diode Goto-pair sense amp biased at 0.2 V
idea: A crystal radio works with almost no power. Build each sense amp as a Goto pair, two series Esaki tunnel diodes (e.g., Si/SiGe or III-V on the periphery wafer) biased in their negative-resistance region at ~0.2 V; the bitline signal tips the pair into one of two stable states within picoseconds, with no high-voltage cross-coupled latch.
why: SA latch energy scales with V2: 0.2 V instead of ~1 V is ~25x less latch energy and allows a low-swing bitline; 10x on sensing energy even after diode peak-current overhead; risk is diode uniformity and integration.

title: Igloo: 77 K memory tier runs sensing at half voltage
idea: Keep memory cold like an igloo: put a capacity-tier DRAM in a liquid-nitrogen bath at 77 K, where access-transistor leakage falls by orders of magnitude (refresh nearly vanishes), wire resistance drops ~5x and threshold voltages can be retargeted, so VARY runs at ~0.5 V and VPP at ~1.5 V with periphery at 0.4 V.
why: CV2 terms fall ~4x, wordline ~4x, refresh ~100x, and lower wire resistance shrinks drivers; net ~10x per access at the device even after amortized cryocooler overhead at data-centre scale is debated.

title: Dumbwaiter: per-mat vertical bond shafts replace global data buses
idea: A dumbwaiter carries food straight up to each floor instead of through the halls. Give every mat its own column of hybrid bonds to a logic die stacked directly above, so data leaves the local sense amps vertically over ~10 um instead of crossing mm-long global I/O lines, serializers and the PHY.
why: On-die global I/O plus the PHY are ~40-60% of DDR access energy (10-20 pJ/bit, fact 5); a vertical shaft at ~0.05-0.1 pJ/bit cuts per-access energy ~10x for the data path.

title: Trampoline: segmented plate-line bounce restores cells, bitlines swing 0.25 V
idea: Bounce the cell up from below like a trampoline: segment the normally common cell plate into per-row-segment plate lines; bitlines swing only ~0.25 V during sense, and restore happens by pulsing the segment's plate so the storage node is bootstrapped back to a full level through capacitive coupling, as in FeRAM plate-pulse schemes.
why: Bitline swing falls ~4x (energy ~4-8x) and restore charge moves through one plate segment rather than 8k bitlines; ~10x on array energy; risks are plate-to-plate coupling and disturb of unselected cells.

title: Pogo stick: ferroelectric negative capacitance cancels bitline load
idea: A pogo spring returns energy instead of absorbing it. Put a thin HZO negative-capacitance element in series at each SA input so the bitline-plus-NC network shows a much smaller effective capacitance during charge sharing, raising the signal per unit charge and letting the array run at ~0.4-0.5 V.
why: Effective C_BL ~3-5x lower and VARY ~2x lower give ~10x on bitline energy if a stable, hysteresis-free NC regime can be held; physics is unproven at speed.

title: Empty mailbox flag: zero-word detect skips internal data toggling
idea: Don't open the mailbox if it is empty: a wired-NOR at each local sense-amp group flags all-zero 64-bit words, and the chip sends a 1-bit flag on a side line instead of toggling the global data lines, I/O drivers and PHY; ReLU activations, sparse weights and fresh pages are 50-90% zeros.
why: Internal data movement plus I/O is most of access energy; skipping zero words cuts it ~2-10x depending on sparsity, ~10x on sparse AI tensors.

title: Tin-can telephone: 60 mV ground-referenced global data lines
idea: A tin-can telephone carries a voice on a whisper of energy. Drive the mm-long on-die global data lines with ground-referenced ~60 mV swings from capacitively divided drivers and receive with clocked offset-trimmed sense amps, instead of full 1.1 V CMOS swings.
why: Global data-line energy scales with swing x supply: 60 mV vs ~1 V cuts it ~10-15x; global I/O is ~20-30% of DRAM access energy.

title: Impressionist painting: low-swing lossy sensing for low-order bit planes
idea: An impressionist painting only needs the broad strokes right. Store AI tensors so the low-order bit planes live in dedicated mats that run at VARY ~0.4 V and short sense times with an allowed raw bit error rate of ~1e-4, while sign and exponent planes run at full margin with ECC.
why: ~6x less CV2 energy on the 50-75% of bits that are low-order, about 10x on those mats, with negligible model-accuracy loss from LSB flips; a precision-aware access mode is needed in the controller.

title: Coin-counting machine: multi-row charge summation read by bitline ADC
idea: A coin counter weighs the pile instead of counting coins one at a time: activate up to 8 rows of a bit-plane at once so their cell charges sum on each bitline, then digitize the analog sum with a 3-bit SAR built from the SA's reference caps, returning popcounts or dot-product partial sums rather than raw bits.
why: One activation replaces 8 activations plus 8x data transfer for reductions and binary/ternary dot products; ~10-30x less energy per useful operation; risks are cell variation and destroyed data needing copy rows.

title: Venetian blinds: bit-plane layout fetches only requested precision bits
idea: Tilt Venetian blinds to let in only the light you want. Store tensors transposed into bit-planes across column groups, with a precision-select field in the column command so a 4-bit or 8-bit inference read opens only those planes' micro-rows and moves only those bits, not the full 16-bit words.
why: Activation plus transfer energy scales with bits actually needed: 2-4x from precision alone, and >10x when combined with micro-row activation that already removes overfetch.

title: Ice rink: Josephson comparators sense cryogenic DRAM bitlines
idea: Glide without friction: at 4 K, read DRAM bitlines with Josephson-junction quantum-flux-parametron or SFQ comparators that switch on ~1e-19 J, driving superconducting passive lines to the processor, while the DRAM array runs at ~0.3 V with near-zero leakage and no refresh.
why: Sensing and data-movement energy falls by orders of magnitude at the device; even with cryocooler overhead (~400 W/W at 4 K) this aims at ~10x per access for quantum/superconducting computer memory.

title: Hourglass flip: precharge-free sensing starts from last value
idea: An hourglass is never reset, just flipped. Skip bitline equalization: each bitline starts from whichever rail its last sensed value left it at, a 1-bit tag per bitline group tells the SA to use a high-side or low-side reference, and a cell matching the rail moves no charge, so bitlines toggle only when data changes.
why: Precharge and equalize charge per activation becomes proportional to data change rate; for correlated or zero-heavy data (50-90% unchanged) bitline energy falls ~3-10x.

title: Limbo bar: back-gate pulse lowers wordline voltage to 1.2 V
idea: Lower the bar instead of jumping higher: give each mat's vertical access transistors a shared back gate held negative in retention (high Vt, low leakage) and pulsed positive only for the accessed mat during activation, so the front wordline needs ~1.2 V instead of ~3 V and can run straight from VDD without charge pumps.
why: Wordline energy falls ~(3/1.2)2 = 6x and pump inefficiency (~3x) disappears, ~15x on the wordline component and the voltage floor (fact 10); back-gate RC sets the activation latency.

title: Fridge magnets: inductive coupling links replace TSVs in stacks
idea: Stick dies together like fridge magnets: replace HBM TSVs with on-die coils that couple data inductively between thinned stacked dies at ~1 Gb/s per coil and ~0.05-0.1 pJ/bit, so no TSV keep-out zones or through-silicon etch are needed.
why: Die-to-die energy ~10x below today's TSV plus PHY paths, and removes the TSV area/yield tax (fact 6: ~3x area per bit, 20-30% yield loss).

title: Motion-sensor porch light: clockless periphery wakes only on command
idea: A porch light stays dark until someone walks up. Remove the always-on DLL and replace it with source-synchronous strobes, bias command receivers only when chip-select toggles, and replace idling charge pumps with reservoir capacitors recharged right after each burst, so the periphery draws near zero between accesses.
why: At 10-30% utilization, background power (DLL, receivers, pumps) is 40-60% of energy per access; making it event-driven cuts energy per access ~3-10x for lightly loaded memory tiers.
